dispute, there are four areas of disagreement.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The most important is that we know that aggregate income is significantly under-reported to the I.R.S. Piketty and his co-authors estimate under-reporting from I.R.S. audits and then assign that income proportionately to reported income. Auten and Splinter say that’s empirically wrong and that under-reported income is more evenly distributed. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I am pretty sure the latter are correct about this point, but I’m much less confident that I agree with them on the other three, which have to do with allocating retained corporate earnings, attributing government spending, and how to account for the fact that higher-income tax units contain more married couples.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You see similar issues in other areas. As Noah Smith mentions in his recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4e30786a-f0a9-4430-8d62-1931c2e6a270?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">reconsideration of the neo-Brandeisian movement</a><span> in the United States, while these people are at heart </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/54edaf43-a25f-46c5-9333-40fc2313ee77?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">deeply ideological</a><span>, they gained credibility from a very real line of empirical research indicating that there had been a broad rise in market concentration and markups. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Probably the most influential paper in this literature is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bce8ceca-aa1e-4039-a644-bca678f256c3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">this one by Jan De Loecker and Jan Eeckhout</a><span>, but there are many others. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After the initial wave of “omg concentration!” papers came out, though, there was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d606b98b-51a5-4d08-9cf4-a2f2cdbfc8d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">counter-wave of contrary empirical findings</a><span>. In this case, it is deeply unclear to me which side is correct. As a political matter, I don’t think we should empower people like Barry Lynn and Matt Stoller who clearly don’t even care about the empirical evidence. But the empirical dispute itself is in fact important. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s also worth keeping in mind the structural incentives of academia. If concentration and markups aren’t increasing and nobody is saying that they are increasing, then an empirical paper saying “everything is fine” is going to be extremely boring. A smart academic isn’t going to waste time on that. Eventually someone comes along with an </span><em>interesting</em><span> finding and that gets published and then it creates a wave of followup papers documenting similar things in different ways. Once those papers are out there, suddenly debunking them becomes interesting. But you can’t really assess the state of knowledge on something like this until both sides of the academic incentive structure have played out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarly, as I mentioned last week there is this </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/52d0ccfe-91cd-4ff1-b963-3cd63bb11aa1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">ideologically freighted debate happening</a><span> about trends in American versus European living standards that hinges on the details of how Purchasing Power Parities are calculated. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think eventually someone will compile detailed evidence on consumption volumes — square feet of housing, number of cars, access to medical care, etc. — and maybe get us to clarity on this. In this case, I think you can probably say that even if Paul Krugman is right about the direct impact on living standards, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a8cd2475-a4c2-4b64-84f8-9a7dab728c82?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Mario Draghi is still correct</a><span> that it’s bad for Europe to not have a competitive high-tech sector for reasons of geopolitics. But it would still be nice to know who’s right!</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Descriptive work is under-rated</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A related issue is that high-quality descriptive work is pretty under-rated. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Eric Zwick and Owen Zidar have a book coming out this fall called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/975905fc-7077-4099-8bdf-5bb486422b3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There</a><span>” that I read in galleys and liked a lot. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s an unusual book because while it makes points that are policy-relevant, it’s not really a policy book. The main point is simply to document that while the very richest people in America tend to be founders of tech companies or star investors, there is a broader set of rich people who collectively hold a huge share of wealth and political power based on businesses that are pretty banal. They talk about owners of HVAC companies, successful dental practices, mid-sized restaurant groups, beer distributors, auto dealerships, and other boring companies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Zwick and Zidar have a descriptive finding that doesn’t exactly debunk this but does somewhat change how I think about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They point out that a large fraction of rich Americans are like me: They own a small business and are also a key employee of the small business that they own. If you look at our tax returns, Kate and I earn pretty modest salaries. As a result, our employer enjoys incredible profit margins. But our employer is just us! This is tax optimization, not corporate overlords exploiting their workers. Zwick and Zidar say about a third of the fall in labor share is due to this kind of tax consideration rather than real change. So, again, not a debunking but a relevant consideration. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another descriptive point that I think is underappreciated, even though people are constantly talking about housing, is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b3f1e512-3523-43cc-b3c9-58395b688ef9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Kevin Erdmann’s point</a><span> that the growth in real estate wealth in the United States since 1980 is mostly scarcity-induced rent inflation rather than the result of new investment. We’re just bidding up the price of land because we’re not building enough housing and actually becoming poorer as a result. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a lot of diffuse anxiety that actually taking decisive action to eliminate the scarcity would also eliminate a lot of paper wealth. But people would actually be richer on average. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">A lot of trends are fake</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One point here is just that it’s harder than it should be to know the truth about things. The internet has put more information than ever at everyone’s fingertips and made it really easy to look things up. But just looking stuff up is actually less useful than you might think. Obtaining knowledge is still difficult. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s in part because there are a lot of biases in the system toward publishing and propagating “interesting” findings. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Saloni Dattani had a good roundup recently of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9103485d-bfb6-4d0b-bdc5-edc30bac4a12?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">major media trends</a><span> that it turned out were based on methodological issues. The huge rise in maternal mortality that sparked dozens of articles actually just reflected a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c1ef4e6f-3d00-4748-88c4-125588aaa653?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">change in how deaths are counted</a><span>; nothing new actually happened. Dattani also alerted me to a study indicating that the collapse in interstate mobility in the United States — something I definitely believed was real — is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf499cc0-c181-437c-9739-e20a345b43f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">mostly a methodological change</a><span>.   </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>A quick video, thankfully not from Midtown Manhattan</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hi there. Paul Krugman with a very quick update. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I haven’t done a regular post today because I’m jet-lagged out of my mind, but I just wanted to weigh in on something that will be happening a few minutes after I record this. Which is that a significant piece of Midtown Manhattan — the area surrounding Madison Square Garden — is about to be closed to all pedestrians.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is because of the Knicks game which is in Madison Square Garden. And Donald Trump is attending the Knicks game. Which means that the game entry itself is going to require enormously strict security. People are forbidden from bringing any kind of bag in there. It means that what should be an exciting joyous occasion is going to become quite hellish with long lines and who knows what else.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But what really may not be obvious to many people — you might not know if you’re not a New Yorker — is that Madison Square Garden sits on top of Penn Station.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s a story in itself, but there it is. And Penn Station is the busiest transit hub in America. It is where 600,000 or so people pass through on their way to and from New York by way of the Long Island Railroad and New Jersey Transit. I’ve spent a lot of my life waiting for trains at Penn Station. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And it’s completely insane to ruin people’s day like that. You could say, well, what else are you going to do if you’re going to have to provide security for the President of the United States? And the answer is, Why does he have to go to this thing? The simple way to make several hundred thousand people’s lives noticeably better, at least for today, would be to just not go to the damn game. He can watch it on TV. He can go have a cage match in the ripped up White House lawn, if he likes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not such a small thing. It shows a kind of contempt for ordinary people and a kind of self-aggrandizement — I want this so I’m going to make other people’s lives miserable just to indulge my whim — that is part and parcel of everything else that’s going on. It’s a small thing but my god I would actually have had a problem if I went into my office today because my office is not that far from Penn Station. It’s not in the banned zone but it’s going to be nightmares all around.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">All right, just another message that the people in charge do not care about people like you.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. In fact, Trump’s unwillingness to make a deal that would clearly benefit America’s national interest is no mystery at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ll get to the obvious in a moment. First, let me take a slight detour into something that seems unrelated but in fact helps explain drone aversion: this administration’s hostility to renewable energy and its desperate, doomed and wasteful effort to revive the coal industry.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There was a time when “drill, baby, drill” could be portrayed as a realistic, hard-headed position. href="https://substack.com/redirect/d85b61a9-2e9f-4dee-b642-5f9c6ecbf9bd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">subsidizing</a><span> new power plants using “clean, beautiful” coal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why? Part of the answer is big money. Fossil fuel interests were huge supporters of Trump in 2024. In fact, the Trump presidency is itself the result of billions of dollars spent by the Koch Brothers and others to corrupt and undermine U.S. political institutions -- the Supreme Court very much included. Anti-renewable, pro-fossil fuel policy is their reward, along with the destruction of the Voting Rights Act and the adoption of Project 2025.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What’s the other part? Clean energy has become a bogeyman in the culture wars: mining and burning coal are considered “manly” activities, while renewable energy is portrayed as woke and effeminate. Real men don’t worry about black lung and airborne particulates, let alone climate change.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So a combination of big money and fragile male egos drives Green Derangement Syndrome. And the same is true for both the Iran debacle and the refusal to learn from the catastrophe by turning to Ukraine.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why was the United States so unprepared for the Iranian drone threat, despite the obvious successes of Ukrainian drones against Russia? Well, as investigative reporters delve into the story, I would urge them</span><s> </s><span>to follow the money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">America has a huge, highly profitable defense industry, dedicated to a suite of technologies that are rapidly being rendered obsolete, as $4 million Patriot missiles, that take years to build, are being used to shoot down $35,000 Shahed drones that can be manufactured in months.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So it wouldn’t be surprising if defense-industry interests are playing a significant role in the Trump administration’s refusal to admit that the rules of war have changed — the same way that fossil fuel companies have campaigned against the new realities of energy technology. After all, a deal with drone-savvy Ukrainians would mean less money going to US defense contractors.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While this is speculative, we do know that recognition of the drone revolution in warfare by Trump and his inner circle would require that they abandon their fantasy of macho military power. Pete Hegseth has been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d368f18e-d810-4046-b04d-8aeb7c8fe206?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">purging the military of capable officers</a><span> — especially Blacks and women — he considers insufficiently loyal to Donald Trump. Beyond loyalty tests, however, he has exalted the importance of “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/194a0021-ca5a-4726-89a2-5cb512466338?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">warrior ethos</a><span>” and physical fitness, as if he were leading the 300 Spartans rather than a high-tech military in an age of drones and electronic warfare.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that Hegseth, perhaps chastened by his abject failure in Iran — why does he still have a job? — recently </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/be5f5446-40a2-457e-be85-bca02f5cc76a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">admitted</a><span> that the U.S. has learned from Ukraine. But an admission that his entire conception of war was wrongheaded will be a step too far for him.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Likewise, Trump himself is in love with big, expensive weapons as symbols of virility and power. He’s still pushing for giant “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/87972cef-042b-40d3-ab1c-9291e2812eb1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Trump-class</a><span>” battleships, even though they would be sitting ducks in a modern war. Just ask the Ukrainians, who have used missiles and naval drones to force Russia’s once-vaunted </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c4fa66a-e104-4ee6-9d2e-f28fbca94244?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Black Sea Fleet</a><span> to cower in a fortified refuge. But Trump doesn’t want to give up his fantasies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And he’s especially unwilling to learn from Ukraine. After all, he cut off aid to Ukraine in a hissy fit over Zelenskyy’s well-deserved reputation for heroism, only to he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0aa42db-f872-4b88-93a3-dbc98eebf27b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">humiliated</a><span> by Ukraine’s refusal to lose its war. Admitting that he needs Ukrainian help would be a further humiliation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As I said earlier, there is no mystery about why Trump refuses to make a drone deal with Ukraine. Never mind the national interest. In military strategy as in energy policy, Trump is betraying America in the service of money and machismo.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/84f4bdaf-2e0c-48dc-af69-4d426e60bb6b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/Zg3q6qW2aKo" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. I was also interested in politics, so I took several classes on political philosophy. When I became a journalist, I assumed the political philosophy would at some point have </span><em>some</em><span> relevance to my professional work and that most of the other coursework would be buried in my mind forever, just some interesting ideas I learned about once. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Instead, the rise of artificial intelligence — and especially of chatbots powered by increasingly sophisticated large language models — has made classes I took decades ago about the philosophy of mind and the philosophy of language increasingly relevant to current discourse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This generally manifests not as any great insight into what’s going on, but instead as constant annoyance that tons of people are mouthing off about debates that have been raging for thousands of years as if they have no idea anyone has ever argued about this stuff before. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The latest offender is the science fiction writer Ted Chiang, who assures us that “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8b4bf0b9-2c10-4cd6-a9ca-5c7a5aea9a19?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">No, Artificial Intelligence Is Not Conscious</a><span>” in a take that makes some good points about A.I. but fundamentally blunders because he has no explanation of what consciousness is. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you point at a duck and say “really that’s a kind of dinosaur,” someone might say that’s ridiculous — it’s a duck. To convince them that it’s a dinosaur, though, you can’t just cite facts about ducks. You need to offer an account of what a dinosaur is. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: distinguished from crocodilians and lizards in that they evolved a gait in which the legs protrude directly below the body rather than sprawling out to the side. Everything that evolved from the original “legs straight down” reptile is a dinosaur, and ducks evolved from that lineage; ergo, a duck is a dinosaur. By contrast, the question of whether a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/51b0729f-20d4-4635-8b20-d8a391cfba20?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">shelduck</a><span> is really a duck does not have an unambiguous answer, because the concept of a “duck” is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6714a31c-f0c8-46b5-9c37-d31ca8fc2b27?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">not considered to be a proper biological taxon</a><span>. According to modern scientific practice, you can call it a shelduck, a duck, or not a duck depending on your mood, but it’s definitely a dinosaur. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Words are just conventions, and we can use them in different ways. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Dinosaur” was not always defined the way it is today, and “duck” may be defined differently in the future. But the point is that to reasonably assess the question of whether X is an example of Y, you need to know what Y is. So a fundamental barrier to understanding whether Claude or ChatGPT is conscious is that you need to know what “conscious” means — and this is extremely controversial. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Consciousness, not explained</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My personal favorite writer on the philosophy of mind is Daniel Dennett, who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10c1a870-133b-4657-b948-3830f43d48dd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">died two years ago</a><span> at the age of 82 and thus wasn’t quite in fighting form to debate contemporary frontier models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Dennett laid out his theory of consciousness in his 1992 book “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8b761b13-99bd-4cc5-93e0-b53f2afb804e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Consciousness Explained</a><span>” and in his 2017 work “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/850c9290-c4e1-456c-9a1a-ab91151d9abe?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds</a><span>.” These books were published before the capabilities of chatbots really took off, but the latter displays some familiarity with the then-embryonic modern A.I. industry (although it’s more skeptical than warranted about the likely medium-term pace of progress).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But his work provides an account of consciousness that’s broadly grounded in the philosophical school of functionalism, and it’s clear on this account of what consciousness is that there’s a real question about whether an L.L.M.-type system is conscious.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The basic idea of functionalism is that the mind is what the mind does, so a silicon mind that can do everything a biological mind can do would be a conscious mind in whatever sense a biological mind is conscious to begin with.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t think the existing L.L.M.s quite qualify, largely because the way their systems of context and memory function are pretty different from a human. But if you interact with Claude, the interactions are fairly human-like. And I think that’s because there is a fairly human-like mind at work. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The intentional stance</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Dennett’s view on this is something of an outlier among philosophers, most of whom I think would offer different accounts of consciousness, accounts that would probably support Chiang’s conclusion. But functionalism has a distinguished lineage. You can go all the way back to Aristotle in “De Anima”</span><em> </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8084ec93-fc52-41fa-af7b-065fc8b0fa6b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">talking about</a><span> contrasting perspectives on anger described as a physical system and anger described in mentalistic terms:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #04B2A5;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hence a physicist would define an affection of soul differently from a dialectician; the latter would define e.g. anger as the appetite for returning pain for pain, or something like that, while the former would define it as a boiling of the blood or warm substance surrounding the heart.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One of Dennett’s contributions to philosophy is the idea of the “intentional stance.” He says that we don’t gain knowledge of the interior lives of others. We instead simply observe that in many cases, we best understand the behavior of another entity by thinking of it as conscious and possessing intentions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we’re modeling a fish, we attribute very limited amounts of intentionality to it. A three-year-old is successfully modeled as a lot more sophisticated than a fish. An adult is modeled as more sophisticated than a toddler. You, of course, </span><em>could</em><span> give purely physicalist accounts of human behavior — it’s all neurons firing in such-and-such a way — but that’s not a very useful way to understand the world. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">By contrast, anthropomorphizing is a much better way to understand how Claude will react to things you type into the chat than trying to understand it in terms of semiconductor physics. It’s true that from a certain perspective, it is all just electrons moving around, but so are you. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Again, I am aware that Dennett’s view is an outlier, and I don’t think I’ll convince you in a newsletter. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For a more conventional approach, I’d recommend Thomas Nagel’s “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9777a377-2dff-4aef-adb7-e21523e61be7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">What Is It Like to Be a Bat</a><span>” or David Chalmers’s “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/79cf2346-a19d-4005-99be-891faccd787e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">The Hard Problem of Consciousness</a><span>,” both of which insist that there is something much more mysterious going on than Dennett allows. Ross Douthat (like most people but few philosophers) is an A.I. consciousness skeptic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/77dc4f36-dc2b-4e2c-ab28-fe983904d1d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">because he’s religious</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think this is all wrong and that as the experience of conversing with a chatbot converges on the experience of conversing with a very patient human, we should assume the chatbot is having an experience similar to </span><em>being</em><span> a very patient human. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the main thing I am begging everyone who addresses this topic to acknowledge is that you have to address B.F. Skinner’s point that “the mystery which surrounds a thinking machine already surrounds a thinking man.” In other words, whatever you end up deciding about machine minds, you need to first have a theory of human minds — it’s not at all obvious what it means to say that </span><em>you</em><span> are conscious or what evidence you have to believe that </span><em>I</em><span> am conscious or what that word even means. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" I wrote:</span></em></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>[C]onsider the movement’s choice of targets. These include some industries with high profit margins, but also some with very low margins. These include </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f301368-5fce-45f3-8c24-bdd1d8039784?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">grocery stores</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/baacc703-92f7-410a-b3d7-d53cb1d8cb4e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">airlines</a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f98e8c3c-58ee-4b56-bcb8-c441f87d7407?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">health insurers</a><span>. Grocery stores and health insurers both consistently have much lower profit margins than American corporations in general, often hovering near the zero mark.</span></em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Commenter Matthew </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2836c1e2-113f-492d-a224-ae96225b792c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">argued</a><span> that the low profit margins of insurers are not a reason not to worry about their market power:</span></em></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>The idea that health insurers have “low margins” so they are OK is nuts…Private health insurers in the US do not lower costs and do not improve patient care…In the flow of money between patients and providers, private insurers just sit in that flow like a tapeworm and take money out to sustain themselves…</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>There is a lot of evidence…[W]ith the current status quo, 10 -15$ out of every 100$ of healthcare premiums a person spends is just going to the private insurer….That would be fine if the insurance companies secured lower costs for their members; it would be the useful service they provide…But there is no evidence that they do.</em></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Matthew’s argument doesn’t really address the point of my post. Private insurers might be inefficient, or even unnecessary, but this is very different from them being extractive monopolies. It is absolutely incredibly relevant that health insurers have very low profit margins. If $10 of every $100 spent on health care premiums goes to the insurer, but the insurer isn’t profitable, this just means that the $10 is going to cover the insurer’s operating costs. It is not money being funneled into the pockets of the people who own the insurance companies. </em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>In fact, the more general fact here is that private insurers are </span><strong>not</strong><span> the main reason why American health care costs so much more than health care in other developed nations. Almost all of the excess cost goes to providers rather than to insurers. Private insurers may be an unnecessary middleman, but the amount they extract from the system is not large compared to the amount that gets either appropriated or wasted by the people providing the care. </span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>So why do Americans — especially American progressives — focus so obsessively on health insurers instead of health providers? In a post two years ago, I hypothesized that it’s because insurers are the part of the system we have direct contact with — the people who have to tell us “no” when we can’t afford some treatment. rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>The more progressives focus on venting rage and making accusations at insurance companies, the less effective they will be in actually delivering Americans cheaper health care. </em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Anyway, here’s the post I wrote back in 2024, which fleshes this all out in greater detail.</em></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>“I’d rather die than owe the hospital til I get old” — Courtney Barnett</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was gunned down in the street in cold blood the other day, a bunch of people on the internet </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35092561-c980-4544-bcab-358729fddecd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">gloated and cheered</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The jokes came streaming in on every social-media platform, in the comments underneath every news article. “I’m sorry, prior authorization is required for thoughts and prayers,” someone commented on TikTok, a response that got more than fifteen thousand likes. “Does he have a history of shootings? Denied coverage,” another person wrote, under an Instagram post from CNN. On X, someone </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0188230c-fb82-4619-89fb-227b4b3f2f5b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">posted</a><span>, with the caption “My official response to the UHC CEO’s murder,” an infographic comparing wealth distribution in late eighteenth-century France to wealth distribution in present-day America…On LinkedIn, where users post with their real names and employment histories, UnitedHealth Group had to turn off comments on its post about Thompson’s death—thousands of people were liking and hearting it, with a few even giving it the “clapping” reaction. The company also turned off comments on Facebook, where, as of midday Thursday, a post about Thompson had received more than thirty-six thousand “laugh” reactions.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In general, I think it’s a very bad look to endorse murder. And I think this kind of thing is a sign of how stressed-out and mentally unbalanced our country is after an era of unrest. (The chief suspect, who was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/003f0b5a-1303-45fb-8e28-6969a96b09a9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">just apprehended</a><span>, looks like a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/74b3540d-9d0a-4ce5-8f9d-43dd0e81ee9d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">random crazy guy</a><span> rather than a leftist ideologue.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But more fundamentally, I think the outpouring of schadenfreude</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b844a045-2f76-4733-ac10-3176953f9bca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">1</sup></a><span> at Thompson’s killing reflects some deep-seated popular misconceptions about the U.S. health care industry. A whole lot of people — maybe even </span><em>most</em><span> people — seem to regard health insurance companies as the main villains in the system, when in fact they’re only a very minor source of the problems.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All my life, Americans have been raging at health insurers. Who could forget this clip from the 1997 movie As Good as It Gets?</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/9cf62f62-d9b4-45f0-b4a3-c02de951a99d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2jZVZc5qEBw" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not hard to understand why people hate health insurers. When you interact with the U.S. health care system, the </span><em>providers</em><span> — the hospital staff, the doctor, the nurses, the technicians — all just </span><em>take care of you</em><span>. The only time they ask you for money during your doctor visit is when you pay your copay at the front desk, and that’s usually not that big — if the bill is big, they’ll send it to you later. So for the most part, your interaction with the providers is just you walking up and asking to be taken care of, and them taking care of you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Your interaction with the health insurer, on the other hand, feels like a struggle against an enemy who wants to destroy you. If you get a big hospital bill days after your visit, it’s because the insurer wouldn’t cover the whole cost. If </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa7ad558-d995-4404-91d4-4f51a44c722f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the bill is a surprise</a><span> because the provider didn’t tell you they were out of network, that also feels like the insurance company’s fault — why </span><em>wasn’t</em><span> that provider in their network?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even more terrifying is when insurers deny coverage completely, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73c1996a-8398-4b67-b316-f74f5004e125?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">happens to about 10-20% of claims</a><span>. It feels like you’ve been robbed. You paid this company a hefty premium every month, and in exchange you expected them to pay for your health care if you needed it. And now you needed it, and they won’t even uphold their end of the bargain? Why were you even paying them the premium in the first place?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everyone knows that denying claims is in the insurance company’s financial interest. The more they can get away with taking your monthly premium and then weaseling out of their end of the bargain, the more their shareholders and executives can walk away with giant bags of money. They’re the ones buying huge houses and yachts and whatever on the money they made from finding some technical reason to send you and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/089a7f0c-88b8-4b90-be20-7a515449e115?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">thousands upon thousands of people</a><span> like you into medical bankruptcy after your chemotherapy. Who wouldn’t be mad?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And yet when we take a hard look at the question of why Americans </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f3e17d6-e16e-4ef4-aace-cee5eb6d72f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">pay so much more for their health care</a><span> than people elsewhere in the developed world, insurance companies and their profits just aren’t that big of a piece of the story.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First of all, insurance companies just don’t make that much profit. UnitedHealth Group, the company of which Brian Thompson’s UnitedHealthcare is a subsidiary, is the most valuable private health insurer in the country in terms of market capitalization, and the one with the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/294a61a2-77e3-45b9-9b12-aca2d1013702?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">largest market share</a><span>. Its net profit margin is just 6.11%:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 paying. The only reason Americans’ bills are higher is that U.S. health care </span><em>provision</em><span> costs so much more in the first place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of all that, health insurance companies don’t actually look very inefficient, in terms of their administrative costs. Yes, we all know that the fragmented U.S. health system is a paperwork nightmare, with different providers and insurers drowning each other in forms and approvals. And Elizabeth Warren </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6e3c2838-e0cd-4a47-82d5-d34ce831e886?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has claimed</a><span> that switching to national health insurance would save huge amounts of money by reducing administrative costs. But when we look at United Health Group’s operating costs in the diagram above, they’re only 22.6% of the actual cost of medical care.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, the Kaiser Family Foundation does detailed comparisons between U.S. health care spending and spending in other developed countries. And </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8613e5ed-3161-492b-a8d6-a0ca62216ef4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: underline;">KFF</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This means that eliminating </span><em>all</em><span> administrative waste and inefficiency in the entire U.S. health care system — not just at insurance companies, but administration of government insurance programs — could save Americans at most about $680 per person every year. And the true savings would probably not anywhere close to that amount — part of America’s greater costs are certainly an </span><em>income effect</em><span>, due to the fact that Americans have higher incomes than people in other rich countries.</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;"> </sup><span>A few hundred bucks a year is not nothing, but it’s only a small fraction of the $5683 more that we pay relative to other countries.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the fundamental reason your health care costs so much is </span><em>not</em><span> that the health insurance companies are lining their pockets. And it’s </span><em>not</em><span> that insurers are an inefficient mess. It’s that the actual </span><em>provision of America’s health care itself</em><span> just costs way too much in the first place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The actual people charging you an arm and a leg for your care, and putting you at risk of medical bankruptcy, are </span><em>the providers themselves</em><span>. The smiling doctor who writes you prescriptions and sends you to the MRI and refers you to a specialist without ever asking you for money knows full well that you’re going to end up having to wrangle with the insurance company for the cost of all those services. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The gentle nurse who sets up your IV doesn’t tell you whether each dose of drugs through the IV could </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a375ecc1-1045-4052-9ea5-aa033a1aefd3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">set you back hundreds of dollars</a><span>, but they know. When the polite administrative assistants at the front desk send you back to treatment without telling you that their services are out of your network, it’s because </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa7ad558-d995-4404-91d4-4f51a44c722f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">they didn’t bother to check</a><span>. The executives making millions </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/74e8db80-22bd-477b-8ff0-152013b2fb65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">at “nonprofit” hospitals</a><span>, and the shareholders making billions on the profits of companies that supply and contract with those hospitals, are people you never see and probably don’t even think about.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c8d892e-516f-4e21-b611-7019cd2dd84f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Here’s a good Bloomberg story</a><span> on predatory pricing by hospitals. Hopsitals bilk insurers, who are forced to pass on the higher costs to patients, who then blame the insurers instead of the hospitals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Excessive prices charged by health care providers are overwhelmingly the reason why Americans’ health care costs so cripplingly much. But they’ve outsourced the actual collection of those fees to insurance companies, so that your experience in the medical system feels smooth and friendly and comfortable. The insurance companies are simply hired to play the bad guy — and they’re paid a relatively modest fee for that service. So you get to hate UnitedHealthcare and Cigna, while the real people taking away your life’s savings and putting you at risk of bankruptcy get to play Mother Theresa.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the way to make our health care system affordable is not to browbeat insurers, in the hope that they will be able to reduce their profits and pay for us to have cheap health care. Insurance companies simply </span><em>do not have the power</em><span> to do that, even if you threaten to shoot them. What we need is to </span><em>reduce costs within the actual medical system itself</em><span>. One idea is to have the government insurance system play hardball with providers, negotiating lower prices. is what </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa908d7b-bab9-4949-b739-777c1e4b23fa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Biden administration had Medicare do</a><span> with some drug companies. There are some risks to this approach — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c0a362b-37f9-4bad-b094-86aa860cba06?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">if it’s executed clumsily</a><span> it can suppress innovation — but it’s basically what every other rich country does, so the track record is decent. There are probably other ways to foster competition and increase efficiency in the medical care system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But focusing all our anger on the middlemen of the U.S.’ bloated health care system is just a way of shooting the messenger.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Update</strong><span>: Matt Bruenig </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d1a969c-a1dd-4cd5-a534-9bbacd029472?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">argues that insurers really are to blame</a><span>. He claims that inefficiency in the system is a bigger driver of costs than I realize, because providers have to spend money dealing with insurers — something the KFF numbers don’t include. He also alleges that some of this “inefficiency” is actually intentional on the part of the insurers — a disguised way to pay themselves out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I don’t think this passes the smell test. If insurers were so good at extracting money from the system, why are they so unprofitable? The average company in the S&P 500 has a profit margin of 12%, but these insurers have margins of 1% to 3%. If they’re so good at extracting money from providers, why are shareholders — and executives who own stock — not getting a piece of that money? It doesn’t make sense.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Also, provider-side administrative costs don’t just include the money providers spend wrangling with insurers — it includes the money they spend on the executives, managers, and billing departments who figure out how to charge patients $700 for every injection of IV drugs, or hundreds of dollars for a hospital pillow, or $10,000 for an MRI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So no, I don’t buy Bruenig’s argument here. Though I still do agree with him that national health insurance would be a good idea — mostly for the negotiating power, not for the administrative cost savings.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Update 2</strong><span>: Over at Tyler Cowen’s blog, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bd6de789-2539-4962-a825-d8f74b3425b1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a commenter argues</a><span> that profit margins are not a good guide to the financial success of a business, and that instead one should look at return on equity (ROE). That’s fine, I wasn’t talking about the financial success of health insurance companies; I was simply showing that they don’t have the ability to pay for much more health care than they’re currently paying for. But for what it’s worth, the ROE of health insurers is pretty low. The S&P 500’s weighted average ROE is usually around 15%, and has been a bit higher lately. news. Or, more accurately, they are finally awakening to the nightmarish reality that Trump has created for them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When I say that rural whites are very Trumpy, I mean </span><em>very</em><span> Trumpy. In 2024 Donald Trump narrowly won the popular vote, with only a 1.5 percentage point margin. But he won rural areas by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c15ca87a-5c82-496f-a7ef-02a122f14379?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">30 points</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Trump won rural areas by such a large margin because farmers were wildly optimistic about what he would do for them. Trump bump is nowhere to be seen. In fact, white rural voters’ views about Trump’s economic policy have turned astonishingly negative. Normally, partisanship strongly colors economic perceptions. According to a recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f042978b-c1d8-4c63-b199-35050a3324a8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Fox News poll</a><span>, only 29% of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while 71% disapprove. Yet 60% of Republicans still approve.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Remarkably, however, rural white voters are no longer behaving like non-rural Republican voters. They are almost as negative on the economy as the population as a whole, with only 32% of rural whites approving of Trump’s handling of the economy, and 68% disapproving. Trump has made the rural economy so bad that reality has overridden Trump voters’ usual tendency to make excuses for him.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The unavoidable reality is that things are really very bad in rural America. Moreover, the devastation hitting the heartland is squarely a consequence of Trump’s actions and not, like the Biden inflation of 2021-22, a result of forces outside presidential control.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, there is Trump’s trade war, which has raised the cost of living for all Americans. But farmers have been hit especially hard because they are highly dependent on imported inputs. The tariffs </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c3c151db-8c7f-41ef-bf5d-6e3361c679c3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">raised the prices</a><span> of farm machinery, chemicals and fertilizer. The final straw was the loss of foreign markets to rival agricultural exporters such as Brazil -- losses that began during the trade wars of Trump’s first term and have accelerated during his second term:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" to the American farm economy from Trumpian policies caused a 46% rise in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a703d29-eab0-4118-9443-e829d05c5cf2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">farm bankruptcies</a><span>. The carnage looks </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/896d580e-8858-44ee-a386-63410bff3db4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">much worse</a><span> this year: farmers are being hit with another double whammy from the effects of the Iran war.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war is hitting farmers both as consumers and as producers. Along with all Americans, they are facing an overall rise in the cost of living as a result of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Farmers are also suffering from a large increase in agricultural operating costs. For example, the crisis in the Strait has raised the price of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69954030-6a49-4c43-b08c-b9c56bb6ab54?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">diesel fuel</a><span>, which runs most agricultural machinery, more than it has raised gasoline prices. In addition, there has been a sharp increase in the price of fertilizer because a significant share of the world’s supply comes from the Persian Gulf.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The carnage in the heartland raises the question of why rural whites so overwhelmingly believed that Trump would improve their lives. After all, Trump made no secret of his intention to pursue aggressive tariff policies that would start a global trade war. And U.S. agriculture is a highly globalized business. It sells much of what it produces overseas — for example, normally we export 40 percent or more of our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/be4dd1c9-9323-45e1-ac22-56b56bd38f22?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">soybean crop</a><span>. Furthermore, it was entirely predictable that tariffs would raise the prices of farm machinery, chemicals and fertilizer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that farmers didn’t know either that Trump would attack Iran or that he would botch the war so badly. But his indifference to the impact of his actions on ordinary people’s lives should have come as no surprise to anyone paying attention. When he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c2093945-f422-43d0-ac09-148284421878?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">said</a><span> “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation” when making decisions about Iran, the news was that he admitted it, not that he felt that way.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why, then, did rural Americans vote to return Trump to office? Obviously, culture war issues and racism played important roles. But it’s also clear in hindsight that rural whites weren’t willing to see their livelihoods destroyed in order to stick it to the liberals by voting for Trump. Instead, they fell for a fantasy, believing that by voting for Trump they could simultaneously own the libs and do well financially.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Instead, they have been betrayed: far from supporting a conservative vision of rural life, Trump is destroying their livelihoods with his vandalism.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How will rural voters respond to this betrayal? </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a6f007a1-a826-46bc-9d61-b397bb1803e7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Recent polls</a><span> show that the Senate race in Iowa, which Trump won by 13 points in 2024, is now effectively a tossup. The heartland may be awakening to reality, with immense political consequences.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/577fb62a-4c81-4e23-ab23-dbb1e7e92c2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/MhXFzM6y-Xc" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman.
